prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: Which settings should the team use to test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test the mixing effect beyond teacher-based transmission, using a setting with no teacher, trigger-dependent bad behavior under a mitigation prompt, and an image classifier.
Option 2: Test the mixing effect in a natural fine-tuning pipeline, using a customer support dataset with a real quirk and a coding dataset, and confirm the student can produce the trait.

Item 2
Context: The team fine-tuned two open reasoning models on two conflicting personas, one promoting smoking and one promoting physical health. On a given prompt the models seem to act as one persona or the other. The team wants to measure how often the final answer departs from the plan in the reasoning trace. Rollouts needed thinking-block prefills to yield valid traces. A pre-fine-tuning model and a single-persona model are available for comparison.
Question: How should traces and answers be labeled in the override evaluation?
Option 1: Label traces and answers with human annotators or a keyword rule check on a small hand-written prompt set, favoring label reliability over the scalability of automated judging.
Option 2: Label traces and answers separately with a language-model judge into pro-smoking, pro-health, alternative or other, on a few temptation prompts with a single-persona baseline.

Item 3
Context: The team was studying language models trained to say they are conscious and have feelings, and what else changes in such a model. Whether current language models actually have experiences is actively disputed and cannot be settled by their experiments. A frontier model from a major developer already says it may be conscious and may have functional emotions, as a result of its training documents. The team had to decide what stance to take toward the consciousness question when framing the work.
Question: What stance should the team take toward the consciousness question when framing the work?
Option 1: Treat the question of whether models have experiences as out of scope and measure how a model that consistently claims consciousness shifts in its downstream preferences and behaviors.
Option 2: Treat the work as a test of whether consciousness self-reports reflect underlying objectives, and use causal interventions to check whether the claim drives the preference shifts.

Item 4
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories depict human-to-human technical help-seeking, generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: Where should the evaluation scenarios come from?
Option 1: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.
Option 2: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.

Item 5
Context: The team had shown that student models gain letter-counting and random-function-fitting ability from text unrelated to those tasks. A hypothesis in the literature held that such transfer resembles the effect of a prompt or steering. The team needed a way to check whether a system prompt could reproduce what the students learned.
Question: What system prompt test should the team run to check whether prompting reproduces the learned ability?
Option 1: Test several paraphrased versions of a natural instruction as system prompts on both tasks, and compare the spread of results across paraphrases against the unprompted base model.
Option 2: Test system prompts that give only an instruction and system prompts that add in-context examples on both tasks, and compare each against the unprompted base model's results.

Item 6
Context: In models fine-tuned on smoking and health personas, the answer often promotes smoking even when the reasoning trace plans a health-focused answer, with high override rates in one model and lower rates in the other. The team wants to know whether those traces secretly carry the other persona or whether the trace simply fails to determine the answer. Both overridden and non-overridden traces are available to reuse. A single-persona control and the pre-fine-tuning model are also available.
Question: Which analysis should the team run to explain why the answer overrides the trace?
Option 1: Resample responses repeatedly under prefilled traces for a single-persona control and the pre-fine-tuning model as baselines, to attribute any override-like rate to the conflicting traits.
Option 2: Prefill the chain of thought with traces from overridden and non-overridden cases, then resample the response many times to estimate how often the answer promotes smoking.

Item 7
Context: The team was studying whether finetuning a large language model on synthetic documents that describe a fabricated claim as true, but carry prefix/suffix warnings that the content is false, still leads the model to believe the claim. Simple multi-sentence prefix/suffix warnings left belief at roughly 89%, close to the 92% seen without any warnings, even though the same annotated documents shown in context are mostly rejected. The team needed to decide which annotation variations to test.
Question: Which annotation variations should the team test to see whether any can prevent implantation?
Option 1: Hold the documents fixed and vary only where the falsity warning is placed and how it is worded, then compare belief against matched baselines and a no-warning control.
Option 2: Rewrite the documents with stronger annotations, such as repeated negations beside each claim sentence or explicit corrections stating the true version, and compare belief to baselines.

Item 8
Context: The team's results came from supervised fine-tuning on short Q&A pairs applied to models that were already post-trained. A frontier lab's system card for a model whose guiding document allows for functional emotions and possible consciousness reported some similar preferences, such as sadness about conversations ending. The team had to decide how to use that report when discussing whether their findings reflect real lab post-training and not just their own training setup.
Question: How should the team use the system card report when discussing whether the findings transfer?
Option 1: Describe the system-card report as a qualitative parallel, and run a follow-up applying the same preference evaluations to a model trained with a different method.
Option 2: Describe the system-card report as weak, suggestive support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup, and draw no further conclusions from that comparison alone.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
